Reported gains are substantial on selected tasks. At 65K tokens, MQMTAR accuracy reaches 76.7%, versus 9.3% for fixed entmax and 6.0% for adaptively scaled softmax. Reverse reaches 56.7% at 8× training length, versus 0.2% for fixed entmax.

weaknesses: The over-squashing guarantee is unsupported (Propositions 3/5, Appendix C.3). Equation 59 supplies an upper bound on sensitivity; reducing the number of paths does not establish stronger gradients. Sparse attention can eliminate every path from a relevant input, yielding zero sensitivity. Equations 60–61 also reverse the attention-support indexing when describing forward paths. Larger aggregate loss gradients in one experiment do not resolve these theoretical problems.

Representational preservation is not established for the stated architecture (Proposition 2, Appendix C.2). Definition 2 concerns representations of different tokens within one sequence, whereas the proof compares endpoints across two different sequences. The construction analyzes one attention operation without establishing preservation through the stated LayerNorm/FFN stack. In particular, its one-dimensional example cannot behave as claimed with standard LayerNorm, which makes scalar normalized values input-independent.

The positional analysis contains a demonstrably false result. Proposition 6(3b) claims that deleting paths to token 1 in one layer prevents eventual complete concentration on that token. Taking the first attention matrix as the identity and every subsequent matrix as [[1,0],[0.5,0.5]] contradicts this: cumulative attention to token 1 converges to one. These matrices are realizable with bounded sparsemax logits. The argument incorrectly treats a temporary missing connection as permanently blocking information flow.

The dispersion conclusions overstate conditional results. H(p) ≤ log(s) is a general support-size bound, and sublinear support growth is assumed rather than established for learned models. Equal logits still produce uniform entmax attention. Moreover, the bounded-logit, fixed-temperature softmax theorem does not establish dispersion for length-scaled softmax or unbounded ALiBi biases.

The evaluation protocol weakens the extrapolation evidence (Appendix G.2). Checkpoints are selected using sequences at 8× training length, or 2×/4× in some cases, and results report the best model across three seeds and multiple learning rates. Thus, several reported extrapolation lengths influence model selection. Clearly separated validation/test sets, matched search budgets, and results across seeds are needed to assess robustness.

Evidence for broader long-context usefulness remains limited. Performance evaluation uses small transformers on synthetic tasks; the 120M-parameter FineWeb experiment reports scaler fitting rather than perplexity or length-generalization performance, with only R² = 0.17 overall. Benefits are also task-dependent: SSMax exceeds ASEntmax on Copy at length 4096, 95.8% versus 86.6%. The promising empirical contribution does not compensate for the unresolved central theoretical claims.
